'''{{ill|Narahara Shrine|ja|奈良波良神社|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Narahara Shrine|qq=}}''' (*Narahara Jinja*) is an auxiliary shrine (*sessha*) of {{ill|Kōtai Jingū|ja|皇大神宮|1=Kōtai Jingū|2=ja|3=皇大神宮|4=zh|5=皇大神宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtai Jingū|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōtai Jingū|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} (the Inner Shrine of the [[Ise Grand Shrine]]), located in {{ill|Tamaki|en|Tamaki|qid=Q1289593|lt=Tamaki|1=Tamaki}}, {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|qid=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture|1=Mie Prefecture}}, Japan. It Ranks 22nd among the auxiliary shrines of the Inner Shrine.<ref>Ujiyamada City Office (1929): pp. 9–11.</ref>

The name "Narahara" means "oak plain," suggesting that the surrounding area was once a plain abundant with [[Nara tree|Nara]] (oak) trees.<ref name="ic">Ise Bunka Publishing (2008): p. 59.</ref><ref name="gk">Gakken Publishing (2013): p. 67.</ref>

== Overview ==
The shrine is located at Yagurado 833, Miyako, {{ill|Tamaki|en|Tamaki|qid=Q1289593|lt=Tamaki|1=Tamaki}}, {{ill|Watarai District|en|Watarai District|qid=Q1131032|lt=Watarai District|1=Watarai District}}, {{ill|Mie Prefecture|en|Mie Prefecture|qid=Q128196|lt=Mie Prefecture|1=Mie Prefecture}}, Japan.<ref name="tm">Tatsumi Publishing (2013): p. 48.</ref> It is situated on gently sloping terrain surrounded by privately owned forests to the east and west.<ref name="sk7"/> The shrine was established by {{ill|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|en|Yamatohime-no-mikoto|qid=Q4388732|lt=Yamatohime-no-mikoto|1=Yamatohime-no-mikoto}}.<ref name="ic"/><ref name="gk"/> The sacred object (*shintai*) of the shrine is a stone.<ref>Kaneko (1983): p. 59.</ref>

=== Shrine Name and location ===
Although officially named '''Narahara Shrine''' (*奈良波良神社*), it is referred to as '''Narahara Shrine''' (*楢原神社*) in the ''Ritual Records of the Imperial Grand Shrine'' (*皇太神宮儀式帳*).<ref name="sk7"/> The name suggests that the area was once covered with oak (*nara*) trees. The shrine is located in Miyako, which was the site of the "Miyako Misono," a sacred rice field (*shinden*) belonging to {{ill|Toyōke Daijingū|ja|豊受大神宮|1=Toyōke Daijingū|2=ja|3=豊受大神宮|4=zh|5=豐受大神宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyōke Daijingū|13=User:Immanuelle/Toyōke Daijingū|comment=enwiki is a redirect}} (the Outer Shrine of Ise).<ref name="ic"/>

According to the ''Seiyō Gorin Ikkyō'' (*勢陽五鈴遺響*), the name "Miyako" (meaning "capital") derives from an ancient plan to relocate the capital to this area. However, this plan was abandoned due to the emergence of Mt. Daibutsu (*大仏山*), leaving only the name to reflect the intended capital.<ref name="sk7"/> While the ''Report on the Investigation of Shikinaisha'' dismisses this as a "baseless theory," it acknowledges the connection between the shrine's name "'''Nara'''hara" and "Miyako" (都, meaning "capital").<ref name="sk7"/> The Tamaki Town Office explains that the old spelling of Miyako was "Miyako" (*宮子*), meaning "child of the shrine," symbolizing the blessings received from the deities.<ref>{{Cite web|language=ja|url=http://www.tamaki-kanko.jp/html/special_jingu-yukari.html|title=巡る神宮ゆかりの地 (Exploring Places Connected to the Grand Shrine)|publisher=Tamaki Town Office, Industrial Promotion Division|work=Nohon Tamaki Tabi|accessdate=2014-06-01|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20140601033540/http://www.tamaki-kanko.jp/html/special_jingu-yukari.html|archivedate=2014-06-01}}</ref>

== Grounds ==
The shrine grounds cover an area of 9,500 square meters.<ref name="sk9">Shikinaisha Research Association, 1990, p. 239.</ref> In ancient times, the grounds spanned approximately 5 chō (≈49,585 m²).<ref name="sk9"/> Although the shrine forest was confiscated during the 1871 [[Uchichiryo Edict]], 6,807 m² were returned in 1892.<ref name="sk9"/> The sacred grove is mainly composed of [[:en:Hinoki cypress|Hinoki cypress]] trees, with some {{ill|Cedar|en|Cedar|qid=Q9213445|lt=Cedar|1=Cedar}} and {{ill|Pine|en|Pine|qid=Q12024|lt=Pine|1=Pine}} mixed in.<ref name="sk9"/>

Within the grounds, there is a natural stone {{ill|Chōzuya|en|Chōzuya|qid=Q1069667|lt=Chōzuya|1=Chōzuya}} (water basin) donated by devotees.<ref name="ic"/> A stone monument erected by the [[:en:Kishu Domain|Kishu Domain]] prohibiting the killing of living beings remains on site.<ref name="gk"/>

The shrine pavilion, located near the center of the grounds, is constructed in the [[Shinmei-zukuri]] style with a {{ill|board roof|en|board roof|qid=Q12368313|lt=board roof|1=Board roof}}. It measures approximately 1.5 meters in length, 1.1 meters in width, and 2.9 meters in height.<ref name="sk0">Shikinaisha Research Association, 1990, p. 240.</ref> It faces south and is enclosed by a single layer of {{ill|Tamagaki|en|Tamagaki|qid=Q3078312|lt=Tamagaki|1=Sacred fences}} fence with a [[Shinmei torii]] gate.<ref name="sk0"/>

== Enshrined deity ==
The enshrined deity is **Narahara Hime-no-Mikoto**.<ref name="ic"/> The deity is referred to as "Narawara Hime-no-Mikoto" in the *Ujiyamada City History*.<ref name="uy">Ujiyamada City Office, 1929, p. 11.</ref> She is considered the daughter of **Ōminakami-no-Mikoto**.<ref name="sk7"/>

Worshipped as the [[Ubusunagami]] (guardian deity) of the region,<ref name="ic"/><ref name="gk"/> she is classified as a [[Kunitsukami]] (earthly deity).<ref name="tm"/> She is revered as the protector of rice field irrigation, sacred fields, and Narahara.<ref name="tm"/> According to tradition, she dedicated a sacred area to protect [[Yamato-hime-no-mikoto]] during her arduous journey.<ref name="tm"/>

== History ==
The shrine is believed to have been founded by Yamato-hime-no-mikoto, as mentioned in the *Kōtaijingu Gishiki-chō*.<ref name="sk7"/> Since this document dates back to 804 (Enryaku 23), the shrine's existence predates this period.<ref name="sk7"/> During the [[:en:Medieval period|Medieval period]], the shrine fell into ruin until it was restored in 1663 (Kanbun 3) through the efforts of **Ōnakatomi Seichō (Kawabe Seichō)**.<ref>Shikinaisha Research Association, 1990, pp. 237, 240.</ref>

There is debate regarding the original shrine site, as the description in the *Kōtaijingu Gishiki-chō* does not align with the current location.<ref name="sk7"/> Some theories suggest the original site was deep in Miyako's mountains,<ref>Shikinaisha Research Association, 1990, pp. 237–238.</ref> while others propose it was at **Jōtō Shrine**.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Course 18: Exploring Satoyama Shrines|url=http://www.isekanko.jp/k-cycling/course18.html|publisher=Ise City Tourism Association|accessdate=2014-06-01}}</ref> Despite these theories, the shrine has remained at its current site since its restoration.<ref name="sk7"/>

The current shrine pavilion was rebuilt on October 8, 1980.<ref name="sk9"/>

== Rituals ==
Although there is no resident [[Kannushi]] (Shinto priest), one **Ikanushi** is appointed to manage daily affairs.<ref name="sk89">Shikinaisha Research Association, 1990, pp. 238–239.</ref>

Key rituals include:
- **Kinensai (February 19)**: Prayer for abundant harvest
- **Tsukinamisai (June 19 & December 19)**: Monthly festival
- **Kannamesai (October 19)**: Offering of the first fruits to the deity
- **Niinamesai (November 25)**: Celebration of the new harvest

Additional remote rituals are performed at the **Gojō-den Hall** of the Inner Shrine for New Year’s Day, National Foundation Day (February 11), and other imperial-related festivals.<ref name="sk89"/>

== Surroundings ==
The shrine is located west of the Miyako settlement, adjacent to the Hirose Seikō Tamaki Factory. It can be accessed via a gravel path after descending a slope.<ref>Ise Culture Publishing, 2008, p. 57.</ref> Nearby are several [[kofun]] (ancient Kofuns).<ref>Mie Prefecture Culture Promotion Division, 2012, p. 8.</ref>
* **JR Sangu Line - Taki Station**: Approximately 35-minute walk<ref name="tm"/>.
* **Ise Expressway - Tamaki IC**: About 2 minutes (830 m) by car.
